text.p: The Bank of Portugal said it cut its repo rate by 10 basis points (bp) to 6.90 percent and the draining rate, the rate at which it absorbs excess liquidity, by 40 bp to 6.40 percent, effective Tuesday.
The central bank also cut its emergency lending rate by 50 bp to 8.50 percent, effective Tuesday, the start of a new seven-day commercial bank reserve period.
The draining rate cut exceeded analysts' expectations, but the repo rate cut was in line with their expectations.
Analysts polled by Reuters had expected the Bank of Portugal to cut its draining rate by 15 to 30 bps on Monday.
Some analysts expected a cut in the repo rate of between 10 and 15 bp.
Others felt the central bank could opt to wait until it had a clearer idea on what would be the outcome of 1997 public sector wage negotiations before acting.

The Bank of Portugal offered to inject up to 20 billion escudos of seven-day funds into the money market at a fixed rate of 6.90 percent, 10 bp below the previous rate at which it injected repo funds. Bids must be submitted by 1515 GMT.
The Bank's draining rate has stood at 6.8 percent since April 19. The repo rate was previously eased 10 bp to 7.0 percent on October 21.
Better-than-expected inflation figures for October had increased the Bank's room for manoeuvre, analysts said.

In October, inflation dipped 0.1 percent month-on-month, which brought the year-on-year rate to three percent. The 12-month rolling average, the government's benchmark, eased to 3.2 percent from 3.3 percent in September.
Portuguese bonds were well-supported at all-time highs after the rate cuts, dealers said. The bond market had anticipated cuts in Portuguese rates today.

"Futures and 10-year bonds did not react to the rate cuts, although they are well-supported," said one dealer. "They could rise further, but any increase will be slight and dictated by the trend in Spain."
The Portuguese escudo showed no immediate reaction to the rate cuts. It stood at 101.08/10 per mark at 1444 GMT, compared with 101.09/12 at the opening.
Dealers said the escudo could edge higher against other currencies, including the mark, in the coming days amid optimism over Portugal's economic performance.
